analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to provide seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2005 with 15 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats, the bill was sent to the Senate's labor committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every employer with 15 or more workers to provide at least seven days of paid sick leave a year to full-time employees, with a prorated amount for part-timers, usable for the worker's own illness or to care for a child, spouse, parent, or close family member [S2][S3]. Employers with existing leave policies at least as generous would not have to change them, and no employer could cut existing leave to comply [S2][S3]. The Labor Department would enforce it like wage-and-hour laws, and workers could sue for lost pay [S2][S3]. It never moved past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who have no paid sick days and must choose between their paycheck and their health. The bill's own findings state that 76 percent of the poorest families lack regular sick leave, and fewer than half of workers who do have paid sick leave can use it to care for a sick child [S3]. Women, who the bill notes bear most family caregiving duties, and parents of young children benefit most [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers without paid sick days

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide at least seven days of paid sick leave annually for full-time workers, and a prorated amount for those working at least 20 hours a week or 1,000 hours a year [S2][S3].
Leave covers the worker's own illness, medical diagnosis or preventive care, and caring for a child, parent, spouse, or close family member, and accrued leave carries over year to year [S3].

The bill's findings cite evidence that paid sick leave reduces the spread of contagious illness in schools and child care, cuts emergency care costs by enabling earlier treatment, and reduces the roughly $180 billion a year lost to employees working while sick [S3].

Employers may not discriminate or retaliate against workers for using the leave or counting it against them under no-fault attendance policies, and workers may sue for lost pay plus damages with attorney's fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would bear the cost of providing the paid leave, keeping records, and administering the new requirements. Businesses large enough to reach the 15-employee threshold but operating on thin margins, such as retail and food service, would feel it most. The bill's findings argue these costs are offset by lower turnover, less lost productivity from sick workers coming in anyway, and reduced emergency care use [S3].

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a direct payroll cost for covered employers: seven paid days per full-time employee each year, plus recordkeeping, posted notices, and the possibility of worker lawsuits with the employer paying attorney's fees [S3].

A business crossing the 15-employee threshold faces new liability and administrative rules, and opponents of such mandates have generally argued they can discourage hiring at that margin; the bill attempts to soften this with equivalency for existing leave policies and a floor protecting current benefits, but the cost to employers is real [S3].

Workers seeking leave of more than three consecutive workdays can be required to produce a doctor's certification, which for uninsured workers may itself cost money or time; the bill leaves the mechanics for uninsured workers to regulation rather than solving it directly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to tens of millions of workers who currently lose pay or risk their jobs when they or a child fall ill is large and well documented in the bill's own findings, which also point to employer-side offsets from lower turnover and less productivity lost to employees working sick [S3]. The cost is a genuine new expense for covered employers, concentrated in low-margin service industries. On balance the bill was a straightforward transfer of a modest, predictable benefit to workers at a real but limited cost to employers, and it deliberately preserved more generous existing policies rather than replacing them [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, never received so much as a hearing, and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Healthy Families Act on April 27, 2005, joined by 15 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction; that is the only action recorded.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

The bill would have required employers with 15 or more employees to provide seven days of paid sick leave annually for full-time workers and a prorated amount for part-timers, enforceable by the Secretary of Labor and through private lawsuits.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have been required to provide paid sick days, especially in retail, restaurants, and other large low-margin service industries, are better off because the bill never advanced. Workers without paid sick leave are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Covered employers, especially large service firms

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 15 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Durbin, Mikulski, Murray, Harkin, Dodd, Lautenberg, Corzine, Akaka, Boxer, Feingold, Schumer, and Dayton.

against.name: Sen. Mike Enzi
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee action after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats and none of the 55 Senate Republicans signed on; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and the committee chairmanship, the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees (retail, restaurants, and other large service employers)
industries.note: They would pay for at least seven paid sick days per full-time worker and face new recordkeeping, posting, and lawsuit exposure. Their cost is the workers' gain, so their interest in blocking the bill ran against ordinary workers' interest in getting it passed.

The bill's findings argue paid sick leave lets workers get preventive and early care and reduces emergency room use, meaning more routine visits for doctors and clinics [S3]. Workers using leave for more than three days may need a provider certification, a small billable service [S3].
